# Introduction

Employee turnover presents a significant challenge for organizations due to its financial costs and its impact on productivity, team performance, and organizational knowledge. As organizations increasingly leverage People Analytics to support strategic decision-making, predictive modeling offers an opportunity to identify employees who may be at greater risk of leaving before turnover occurs. Rather than reacting to turnover after it happens, organizations can use predictive insights to implement targeted retention strategies that improve workforce stability while making more effective use of organizational resources.

The purpose of this project is to develop and evaluate machine learning models capable of predicting employee turnover using a simulated human resources dataset. The analysis begins with data preparation and exploratory data analysis to better understand the characteristics of the workforce and identify patterns related to employee turnover. Four classification models will then be developed and compared using several evaluation metrics, including confusion matrices, the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), and Youden's J-index. In addition to predictive performance, model simplicity and interpretability will be considered when selecting a final model for deployment.

Although the primary focus of this project is predictive modeling, the ultimate goal is to support evidence-based talent management decisions. The selected model will therefore be evaluated from both a technical and business perspective. The final report includes documentation intended for a fellow data analyst to facilitate model reproduction and future development, as well as an executive summary that translates the technical findings into actionable recommendations for organizational leaders. Finally, the expected financial impact of implementing targeted employee retention interventions will be estimated using the assumptions provided in the project requirements.

# Data Preprocessing

Before developing predictive models, the dataset was prepared to ensure the data were suitable for analysis. This process included importing the data, examining its structure and quality, identifying any missing values or data issues, and converting variables to the appropriate data types. These preprocessing steps establish a clean and consistent foundation for the exploratory analyses and predictive modeling that follow.

## Load Packages

```{r}
#| label: load-packages
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# Set seed at the beginning of the project for reproducibility.
# Stilson requested seed 42 throughout the final project.
set.seed(42)

# This function checks whether each package is installed.
# If a package is missing, it installs it and then loads it.
install_load_packages <- function(packages) {
  installed <- rownames(installed.packages())
  missing <- setdiff(packages, installed)
  
  if (length(missing) > 0) {
    install.packages(missing, dependencies = TRUE)
  }
  
  suppressPackageStartupMessages(
    invisible(lapply(packages, require, character.only = TRUE))
  )
}

# Core packages for importing, cleaning, exploring, visualizing,
# modeling, evaluating, and interpreting the HR turnover data.
install_load_packages(c(
  # Data import and cleaning
  "readxl", "readr", "dplyr","tibble", "tidyr", "forcats", "janitor", "skimr", "naniar",
  
  # Tables and reporting
  "knitr", "DT", "broom", "gt", "gtsummary",
  
  # Visualization and interpretation
  "ggplot2", "GGally", "corrplot", "vip",
  
  # Modeling and evaluation
  "tidymodels", "rsample", "themis", "probably", "pROC", "yardstick","Boruta",
  
  # Specific model engines
  "randomForest", "ranger", "e1071", "rpart", "rpart.plot",
  
  # Utility packages
  "purrr", "conflicted", "doParallel", "PerformanceAnalytics"
))
```

```{r}

conflict_prefer("filter",     "dplyr")

conflict_prefer("tune",       "tune")
```

## Initial Inspection

```{r}
#| label: initial-inspection

# Look at the column names in the raw imported dataset.
# This satisfies the rubric item for reviewing column names.
colnames(hr_raw)

# Look at the structure of the raw imported dataset.
# This satisfies the rubric item for reviewing data structure.
str(hr_raw)

# View dimensions of the dataset: rows and columns.
dim(hr_raw)

# Preview the first few observations.
head(hr_raw)
```

The initial inspection confirmed that the dataset imported successfully and contained 9,999 employee records across 10 variables. The dataset was stored as a tibble and included a combination of numeric and character variables. Most variables were imported with the expected data types; however, several binary and categorical variables (e.g., `work_accident`, `left`, `promotion_last_5years`, `sales`, and `salary`) will require conversion to factors before modeling. Additionally, the inspection identified one variable name that will be standardized to snake_case during the data cleaning process.

## Data Cleaning

Following the initial inspection, the dataset was cleaned and prepared for analysis. A unique identifier was added to each observation to simplify tracking throughout the modeling process, variable names were standardized to snake_case for consistency, and categorical variables were converted to the appropriate factor data types. These preprocessing steps established a clean and consistent dataset for the remaining analyses.

```{r}
#| label: add-id

# Add a unique ID variable so observations can be tracked later if needed.
hr_data <- hr_raw %>%
  mutate(id = row_number()) %>%
  select(id, everything())
```

```{r}
#| label: clean-names

# clean_names() from {janitor} converts all column names to snake_case,
# removes special characters, and ensures unique names.
# This must run before any column-name references downstream.
hr_data <- hr_data %>%
  clean_names()

cat(colnames(hr_data), sep = ",\n")
```

```{r}
#| label: rename-variables

# Rename variables to improve clarity while preserving their meaning.
# The original variable "sales" represents the employee's department.
hr_data <- hr_data %>%
  rename(
    department = sales
  )

# Display updated column names.
cat(colnames(hr_data), sep = ",\n")
```

```{r}
#| label: convert-variable-types

# Convert categorical variables to factors.
# The outcome variable left is coded 1 = left and 0 = stayed.
# The salary variable is ordered because low, medium, and high have a natural rank.

hr_data <- hr_data %>%
  mutate(
    left = factor(left, levels = c(1, 0), labels = c("left", "stayed")),
    work_accident = factor(work_accident, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("no", "yes")),
    promotion_last_5years = factor(promotion_last_5years, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("no", "yes")),
    department = factor(department),
    salary = factor(salary, levels = c("low", "medium", "high"), ordered = TRUE)
  )

# Check updated variable types.
str(hr_data)
```

Following data cleaning, the dataset was evaluated to verify that the preprocessing steps were successful and that the data were suitable for predictive modeling. The cleaned dataset contained 9,999 employee records and 11 variables, including the newly created ID variable. Variable types were successfully converted to their appropriate formats, with binary and categorical predictors represented as factors and the salary variable retained as an ordered factor to preserve its natural ranking of low, medium, and high.

Summary statistics and frequency tables confirmed that the variables contained the expected values and distributions. Approximately 24% of employees in the dataset had left the organization, while 76% remained employed, indicating a moderate class imbalance that will be considered during model development. The majority of employees had not experienced a work accident (85%) or received a promotion within the previous five years (98%). Employees were distributed across ten departments, with the Sales department representing the largest proportion of the workforce (28%). Nearly half of employees were classified in the low salary category (49%), followed by medium (43%) and high (8%) salary levels.

The numeric variables exhibited appropriate levels of variability for analysis. Continuous variables, including satisfaction level, last evaluation, and average monthly hours, contained numerous unique values, while discrete variables such as number of projects and years spent at the company reflected the expected ranges observed within the organization.

The missing data assessment indicated that no variables contained missing values; therefore, no imputation procedures were required. The near-zero variance assessment identified `promotion_last_5years` as the only predictor with limited variability. Because promotions are naturally infrequent in organizational settings and the variable represents a theoretically meaningful predictor of employee turnover, it was retained for subsequent modeling. No zero-variance predictors were identified. Overall, the dataset demonstrated good data quality and required only minimal preprocessing before proceeding to the exploratory data analysis and predictive modeling stages.

# Exploratory Data Analysis

After preprocessing the dataset, exploratory data analysis was conducted to better understand the distribution of each variable and identify patterns associated with employee turnover. Because no missing values were identified during preprocessing, all analyses presented in this section are based on the complete sample of **9,999 employees** (*N* = 9,999). This section includes variable-level summaries and visualizations, correlation analysis among numeric predictors, and crosstab analyses comparing turnover status across selected categorical predictors. These analyses provide context for model development and help identify potential relationships, data patterns, or collinearity concerns before fitting predictive models.

## Individual Variable Exploration

The exploratory data analysis began by examining each variable individually to better understand its distribution and characteristics. Numeric variables were evaluated using descriptive statistics and graphical summaries, while categorical variables were examined using frequency tables and bar charts. Analyzing each variable independently establishes a baseline understanding of the dataset before investigating relationships among predictors or between predictors and employee turnover.

### Numeric Variables

The numeric variables were evaluated using descriptive statistics and histograms to assess their distributions, central tendencies, variability, and potential outliers. Understanding these characteristics provides insight into the range and shape of each variable before examining relationships among predictors or developing predictive models.

#### Satisfaction Level

```{r}
#| label: summary-satisfaction-level

# Generate summary statistics for employee satisfaction level.
summary(hr_data$satisfaction_level)

# Calculate the standard deviation.
sd(hr_data$satisfaction_level)
```

```{r}
#| label: histogram-satisfaction-level
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-width: 6

# Visualize the distribution of employee satisfaction levels.
ggplot(hr_data, aes(x = satisfaction_level)) +
  geom_histogram(
    bins = 20,
    color = "white",
    fill = "#2A9D8F"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Employee Satisfaction Levels",
    x = "Satisfaction Level",
    y = "Number of Employees"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Employee satisfaction levels ranged from **0.09 to 1.00** (*M* = 0.61, *SD* = 0.25), with a median of **0.64**. The distribution was concentrated in the moderate to high satisfaction range, although a smaller group of employees reported substantially lower satisfaction levels. The mean being slightly lower than the median suggests a modest negative (left) skew, indicating that relatively few employees with low satisfaction reduced the overall average. This pattern suggests that while most employees reported moderate to high satisfaction, a distinct subgroup experienced considerably lower satisfaction, which may warrant further investigation when examine relationship between employee satisfaction and turnover.

## Correlation Analysis

Following the individual examination of each variable, correlation analyses were conducted to evaluate relationships among predictors and identify variables associated with employee turnover. A traditional correlation matrix was used to assess relationships and potential collinearity among numeric predictors. A correlation funnel was then used to binarize both numeric and categorical predictors and compare them with the turnover outcome, allowing patterns across employee groups and numeric ranges to be explored before model development.

### Numeric Predictor Correlations

To evaluate relationships among the numeric predictors, a correlation matrix and corresponding heatmap were examined. These analyses were used to identify potential multicollinearity prior to model development and determine whether any predictors should be removed due to excessively strong correlations.

#### Correlation Matrix

A Pearson correlation matrix was computed using the numeric predictor variables to evaluate the strength and direction of linear relationships among predictors. Examining these relationships provides an initial assessment of potential multicollinearity prior to model development.

```{r}
#| label: correlation-matrix

# Compute the Pearson correlation matrix for the numeric predictor variables.
cor_matrix <- hr_data %>%
  select(
    satisfaction_level,
    last_evaluation,
    number_project,
    average_monthly_hours,
    time_spend_company
  ) %>%
  cor()

cor_matrix
```

#### Correlation Heatmap

To complement the correlation matrix, a heatmap was created to provide a visual representation of the strength and direction of correlations among the numeric predictors. Darker colors indicate stronger positive or negative relationships, while values closer to zero indicate weaker linear associations.

```{r}
#| label: correlation-heatmap
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-width: 6

# Visualize the Pearson correlation matrix.
corrplot(
  cor_matrix,
  method = "color",
  type = "upper",
  order = "original",
  addCoef.col = "black",
  number.cex = 0.8,
  tl.col = "black",
  tl.srt = 45,
  diag = FALSE,
  col = colorRampPalette(c("#2A9D8F", "white", "#E76F51"))(200)
)
```

#### Collinearity Assessment

Examination of the Pearson correlation matrix indicated generally weak to moderate relationships among the numeric predictors. The strongest correlation was observed between **number of projects** and **average monthly hours** (*r* = .42), suggesting that employees assigned more projects generally worked more hours. Moderate positive correlations were also observed between **last evaluation** and **number of projects** (*r* = .35) and between **last evaluation** and **average monthly hours** (*r* = .35). All remaining correlations were relatively weak. Overall, the observed correlations did not indicate evidence of problematic multicollinearity, and all numeric predictors were retained for subsequent analyses and model development.

### Correlation Funnel

The correlation funnel was used to explore relationships between employee turnover and both numeric and categorical predictors. This technique converts predictors into binary features and correlates each resulting feature with the turnover outcome. Correlations farther from zero indicate stronger associations with employee turnover, while the sign indicates the direction of the relationship.

```{r}
#| label: correlation-funnel
#| fig-height: 8
#| waring: false 

#install.packages("correlationfunnel")
library(correlationfunnel)

# Prefer the correlate() function from {correlationfunnel}.
conflict_prefer("correlate", "correlationfunnel")

# Binarize all predictors and correlate them with employee turnover.
hr_data %>%
  select(-id) %>%
  
  # Temporarily recode turnover as 1 = left and 0 = stayed.
  mutate(left = as.numeric(left == "left")) %>%
  
  # Divide numeric predictors into four bins and create binary indicators
  # for numeric ranges and categorical levels.
  binarize(
    n_bins = 4,
    thresh_infreq = 0.01
  ) %>%
  
  # Correlate each binary feature with the turnover outcome.
  correlate(target = left__1) %>%
  
  # Create a static correlation funnel for the PDF report.
  plot_correlation_funnel(interactive = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = "Correlation Funnel — Employee Turnover Predictors"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The correlation funnel provides an initial assessment of the relationships between employee turnover and each predictor by converting variables into binary features and computing their correlations with the turnover outcome. The strongest associations were observed for **low satisfaction levels**, which were positively associated with employee turnover, whereas **high satisfaction levels** were negatively associated with turnover. Employees assigned a greater number of projects and those working longer monthly hours also demonstrated modest positive associations with turnover. In contrast, department membership and promotion history exhibited relatively weak relationships with employee turnover. These findings provide an initial indication of potentially important predictors and will be explored further through crosstab analyses and predictive modeling.

## Crosstab Analyses

To further investigate the relationships between employee turnover and key predictor variables, crosstab analyses were conducted using variables identified as potentially important during the individual variable and correlation analyses. Crosstabs summarize the distribution of employee turnover across groups and provide an intuitive view of how turnover rates differ among employee segments. The selected variables include employee satisfaction, number of projects, salary level, and department.

Overall, these findings indicate that employee satisfaction is strongly associated with employee turnover and support the results of the correlation funnel, suggesting that satisfaction is likely to be an important predictor in the subsequent predictive models.
