Threshold analysis indicated that the Random Forest model achieved its maximum J-Index of 0.960 at a classification threshold of approximately 0.43 to 0.44. This threshold is modestly lower than the default 0.50 cutoff, suggesting that employees should be classified as potential turnover risks once their predicted probability of leaving reaches approximately 43%. At this threshold, the model maintained a strong balance between identifying employees who left and correctly clearing employees who stayed. The predicted probability distribution also demonstrated substantial separation between the two outcome classes, with most employees who stayed receiving probabilities near zero and most employees who left receiving probabilities near one. Although the J-Index-maximizing threshold provides a statistically balanced cutoff, the final deployment threshold will also be evaluated using the assignment’s intervention costs and expected turnover savings.

## Cost Analysis

Predictive performance alone does not determine whether a turnover model provides organizational value. The following analysis applies the assignment’s financial assumptions to estimate the expected costs and savings associated with deploying the Random Forest model across alternative classification thresholds. Each employee identified as likely to leave would receive a \$5,000 intervention, with the intervention expected to prevent turnover 50% of the time. Avoiding one departure saves \$100,000 in turnover costs, resulting in \$95,000 in realized savings when an intervention succeeds. Because unnecessary interventions still consume organizational resources, false-positive costs were also incorporated into the threshold comparison.

```{r}
#| label: cost-setup

# Count the employees who left and stayed in the held-out test set.
test_counts <- rf_test_probs %>%
  count(left, name = "n")

n_left <- test_counts %>%
  filter(left == "left") %>%
  pull(n)

n_stayed <- test_counts %>%
  filter(left == "stayed") %>%
  pull(n)

# Store the financial assumptions provided in the assignment.
turnover_cost <- 100000
intervention_cost <- 5000
intervention_success <- 0.50

# Calculate the expected net value of intervening on one true leaver.
# The intervention cost is incurred whether the intervention succeeds or fails.
expected_value_per_tp <-
  intervention_success * turnover_cost - intervention_cost

cat(
  glue::glue(
    "Employees who left in test set : {n_left}\n",
    "Employees who stayed in test set: {n_stayed}\n",
    "Expected net value per true-positive intervention: ",
    "${scales::comma(expected_value_per_tp)}\n"
  )
)
```

```{r}
#| label: cost-function

# Convert threshold-level sensitivity and specificity into
# expected confusion matrix counts and financial outcomes.
cost_tbl <- threshold_data %>%
  filter(.metric %in% c("sensitivity", "specificity")) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    id_cols = .threshold,
    names_from = .metric,
    values_from = .estimate
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    # Estimate confusion matrix counts at each threshold.
    TP_count = sensitivity * n_left,
    FN_count = (1 - sensitivity) * n_left,
    FP_count = (1 - specificity) * n_stayed,
    TN_count = specificity * n_stayed,

    # Everyone predicted to leave receives the intervention.
    Employees_Intervened = TP_count + FP_count,
    Intervention_Cost =
      Employees_Intervened * intervention_cost,

    # Only half of true-positive interventions are expected
    # to prevent an otherwise expected departure.
    Expected_Retained =
      TP_count * intervention_success,

    Avoided_Turnover_Cost =
      Expected_Retained * turnover_cost,

    # Remaining turnover includes missed leavers and true-positive
    # employees whose intervention is unsuccessful.
    Expected_Remaining_Leavers =
      FN_count + TP_count * (1 - intervention_success),

    Expected_Turnover_Cost =
      Expected_Remaining_Leavers * turnover_cost,

    # Baseline assumes no model and no intervention program.
    Baseline_Turnover_Cost =
      n_left * turnover_cost,

    # Total expected deployment cost and savings versus no program.
    Total_Program_Cost =
      Intervention_Cost + Expected_Turnover_Cost,

    Net_Savings =
      Baseline_Turnover_Cost - Total_Program_Cost,

    # Retain J-Index for comparison with the statistical threshold.
    j_index =
      sensitivity + specificity - 1
  )

# Select the threshold producing the greatest expected net savings.
# If financial results tie, prefer fewer false positives.
max_savings_row <- cost_tbl %>%
  arrange(
    desc(Net_Savings),
    FP_count,
    desc(.threshold)
  ) %>%
  slice(1)

max_savings_threshold <- max_savings_row$.threshold
max_savings_value <- max_savings_row$Net_Savings

cat(
  glue::glue(
    "Maximum expected net savings: ",
    "${scales::comma(round(max_savings_value))}\n",
    "Financially optimal threshold: ",
    "{round(max_savings_threshold, 2)}\n",
    "Expected employees retained: ",
    "{round(max_savings_row$Expected_Retained, 1)}\n",
    "Expected false positives: ",
    "{round(max_savings_row$FP_count, 1)}\n",
    "Employees receiving interventions: ",
    "{round(max_savings_row$Employees_Intervened, 1)}\n"
  )
)
```

Incorporating the estimated costs of employee turnover and targeted retention interventions shifted the optimal Random Forest classification threshold from approximately **0.43**, which maximized J-Index, to **0.30**, which maximized expected financial return. At the 0.30 threshold, approximately **702 employees** would receive a retention intervention, including an estimated **685 employees** who would otherwise leave and only **17 employees** who would have remained without intervention. Assuming the intervention successfully prevents turnover 50% of the time, approximately **342.5 departures** would be avoided. This corresponds to approximately **\$34.25 million** in avoided turnover costs and **\$3.51 million** in intervention costs, yielding an estimated **net savings of \$30.74 million**. Although the threshold that maximizes financial return is lower than the statistically optimal threshold, the relatively small number of unnecessary interventions suggests that the organization can substantially increase expected savings while maintaining an acceptable false-positive rate.

## Variable Importance

To improve interpretability, the finalized models were refit using the full dataset before extracting importance estimates. This provides more stable estimates by using all available observations after model selection and test-set evaluation were complete. Variable importance identifies the predictors the models relied on most heavily when distinguishing employees who left from those who stayed; however, these results should be interpreted as predictive associations rather than causal effects.

```{r}
#| label: create-model-data

# Full labeled dataset used only for post-evaluation refits,
# variable importance, and whole-dataset scoring.
model_data <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  train_data,
  test_data
)
```

```{r}
#| label: fit-full-data

# Create a helper function that finalizes a selected workflow
# and refits it using the complete available dataset.
fit_full <- function(
  wf_results,
  wflow_id_str,
  metric = "j_index"
) {
  
  # Select the correct complete dataset.
  # Weighted workflows require the version containing case_wt.
  full_data <- get_full_data_for_model(wflow_id_str)

  # Identify the best hyperparameter configuration
  # for the selected workflow.
  best_params <- wf_results %>%
    extract_workflow_set_result(wflow_id_str) %>%
    select_best(metric = metric)

  # Finalize the workflow and fit it to the full dataset.
  wf_results %>%
    extract_workflow(wflow_id_str) %>%
    finalize_workflow(best_params) %>%
    fit(full_data)
}
```

```{r}
#| label: vip-logistic
#| fig-height: 5

# Refit the strongest logistic regression workflow
# using the complete dataset.
lr_full_fit <- fit_full(
  race_results,
  best_lr_id
)

# Extract coefficient-based variable importance.
vip_lr <- lr_full_fit %>%
  extract_fit_parsnip() %>%
  vip::vi() %>%
  
  # Translate coefficient direction into turnover language.
  mutate(
    Sign = if_else(
      Sign == "POS",
      "Higher predicted probability of leaving",
      "Lower predicted probability of leaving"
    )
  )

# Display the 20 most influential logistic regression coefficients.
vip_lr %>%
  slice_max(
    order_by = Importance,
    n = 20
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    Variable = forcats::fct_reorder(
      Variable,
      Importance
    )
  ) %>%
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = Importance,
      y = Variable,
      fill = Sign
    )
  ) +
  geom_col() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Logistic Regression — Top 20 Coefficients",
    subtitle = "Direction indicates association with predicted turnover risk",
    x = "Absolute Coefficient Importance",
    y = NULL,
    fill = "Direction"
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: vip-rf
#| fig-height: 5

# Refit the strongest Random Forest workflow
# using the complete dataset.
rf_full_fit <- fit_full(
  race_results,
  best_rf_id
)

# Display the 20 predictors that contributed most
# to the finalized Random Forest model.
vip::vip(
  rf_full_fit$fit$fit$fit,
  geom = "col",
  num_features = 20,
   aesthetics = list(fill = "#2a9d8f")
) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Random Forest — Top 20 Variable Importances",
    subtitle = "Higher values indicate greater contribution to turnover predictions",
    x = "Variable Importance",
    y = NULL
  )
```

Variable importance analyses from both the logistic regression and Random Forest models identified several consistent predictors of employee turnover. Across both modeling approaches, **employee satisfaction**, **time spent at the company**, and **workload-related variables** (e.g., number of projects and average monthly hours) emerged as the most influential predictors of turnover. The Random Forest model placed the greatest emphasis on satisfaction level, number of projects, average monthly hours, last evaluation, and organizational tenure, suggesting that employees' work experiences and workload characteristics contributed more strongly to turnover predictions than compensation level or department membership. The logistic regression model similarly highlighted satisfaction and tenure while also identifying salary level and workplace accidents as influential predictors through their estimated coefficients. Although the two modeling approaches quantify importance differently, the consistency across models increases confidence that these variables represent meaningful predictors of employee turnover. Importantly, variable importance reflects each predictor's contribution to accurate classification and should be interpreted as predictive associations rather than evidence of causal relationships.

# Choosing the Final Model

The Random Forest workflow consistently demonstrated the strongest predictive performance across cross-validation and held-out test evaluation. It achieved the highest overall discrimination, maintained excellent sensitivity and specificity, and generalized well to previously unseen employees. Subsequent threshold optimization and cost analysis indicated that the selected Random Forest model could be deployed at a threshold that balanced predictive performance with organizational costs while producing substantial expected savings. Collectively, these findings support selecting the Random Forest model for organizational deployment.

## Save Final Model

Following evaluation across multiple modeling approaches, the Random Forest model was selected as the final model for deployment. Saving the finalized model as an RDS object preserves the trained workflow, including preprocessing steps and tuned hyperparameters, allowing the model to be reloaded for future scoring without retraining

```{r}
#| label: save-final-model

# Create a folder to store the finalized deployment model.
model_dir <- "models"

dir.create(
  model_dir,
  showWarnings = FALSE,
  recursive = TRUE
)

# Save the finalized Random Forest model.
saveRDS(
  rf_full_fit,
  file.path(model_dir, "random_forest_final_model.rds")
)

# Save the original data split for reproducibility.
saveRDS(
  data_split,
  file.path(model_dir, "data_split.rds")
)

cat("Final model saved to:", model_dir)
```

## Reload Final Model

To confirm reproducibility, the saved Random Forest model was reloaded from the RDS file and used to generate predictions on the held-out test set. Matching performance metrics and prediction outputs verify that the serialized model can be successfully restored and used for future scoring without retraining.

```{r}
#| label: reload-final-model

# Specify the folder containing the saved model.
model_dir <- "models"

# Reload the finalized Random Forest model.
rf_full_fit_reload <- readRDS(
  file.path(model_dir, "random_forest_final_model.rds")
)

# Reload the original train/test split.
data_split_reload <- readRDS(
  file.path(model_dir, "data_split.rds")
)

# Retrieve the held-out test data.
test_data_reload <- testing(data_split_reload)

# Generate predicted probabilities and predicted classes.
reload_preds <- test_data_reload %>%
  bind_cols(
    predict(
      rf_full_fit_reload,
      test_data_reload,
      type = "prob"
    )
  ) %>%
  bind_cols(
    predict(
      rf_full_fit_reload,
      test_data_reload
    )
  )

# Confirm that the reloaded model reproduces the original test-set performance.
bind_rows(
  hard_metrics(
    reload_preds,
    truth = left,
    estimate = .pred_class
  ),
  roc_auc(
    reload_preds,
    truth = left,
    .pred_left
  ),
  pr_auc(
    reload_preds,
    truth = left,
    .pred_left
  )
) %>%
  select(
    .metric,
    .estimate
  ) %>%
  arrange(.metric) %>%
  knitr::kable(
    caption = "Reloaded Random Forest Model — Test-Set Metrics",
    digits = 4
  )

# Display the confusion matrix for the reloaded model.
reload_preds %>%
  conf_mat(
    truth = left,
    estimate = .pred_class
  ) %>%
  autoplot(type = "heatmap") +
  scale_fill_gradient(
    low = "#f8f9fa",
    high = "#e63946"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Reloaded Random Forest Model — Confusion Matrix"
  )
```
